What a win for Tampa. UDFA at quarterback. 0-4, and on the road on a Thursday. Real gutcheck. They rush for 243 and beat a really good Dallas team.

lead_story.research_notes: CONTINUING [Day 2]: Bucs got their first win at 1-4 with an undrafted rookie QB in his second career start, on the road, on a short week, against a 2-2 Dallas team that just hung 34 on the Texans. The funniest angle: Dak told CJ Stroud to 'get some wins' after beating the 0-4 Texans in Week 4, then the Cowboys immediately lost three straight, including tonight to an 0-4 team with a sixth-year college QB who went undrafted. CeeDee Lamb went from a historic 17-catch, 183-yard performance to 2 catches for 9 yards in one week—the biggest receiver collapse you'll see. The stadium worker confrontation is pure gold: Dak heard 'embarrassing' in the hallway, stared the guy down, then called him a 'coward' at the podium for looking away. Jerry Jones left the box early and couldn't even watch the end. Jake Ferguson dropped a crucial 4th-down pass that would've tied the game. Daron Bland dropped an easier pick-six that hit him in the hands. Todd Bowles went for it on 4th down late instead of kicking a field goal to make it a three-score game—got stuffed, gave Dallas life. The Bucs' blueprint: rush for 243 yards (Bucky Irving 21-175-2, first Bucs RB with 150/2 since Bobby Rainey in 2013) and let the undrafted rookie manage the game. Dallas is 2-3, third in the NFC East, 1.5 games back, with an 8% chance to reach the Super Bowl. The internet's already writing their obituary. Brian Schottenheimer said he's considering staff changes. This is the kind of loss that defines a season—and possibly ends one.

supporting_stories.headline: Guardians Force Game 5, Stay Alive

tweets.text:
FINAL: Guardians 9, White Sox 5

The Guardians’ offense has awoken, and it forced a winner-takes-all Game 5 in Cleveland on Saturday for an ALCS berth. José Ramírez and Patrick Bailey homered, and Gavin Williams — the Guardians’ Game 5 starter — came on for the final three outs.

supporting_stories.research_notes: CONTINUING [Day 6, TIER 1 ELIMINATION-ROUND GAME]: Cleveland was on the brink—down 0-2 in the ALDS, facing elimination at home in Game 4. Then José Ramírez took a 100-mph fastball at the top of the zone and sent it out. One swing, 3-2 lead. Patrick Bailey pinch-hit solo shot earlier to get the Guardians on the board. Then the 6th inning happened: Cleveland scored 6 runs, including Ramírez's .010-xBA triple (that's a 1% hit probability) that drove in 3. Bailey came back with a 2-RBI single to give Cleveland the lead for good. The offense that had been silent all series—just 3 runs in the first two games combined—erupted for 9. Gavin Williams, who struck out 11 in Game 2, came on to close the final 3 outs tonight and will start Game 5 on Saturday. The White Sox struck out 19 times. Erick Fedde hit Ramírez, then walked Munetaka Murakami to force in the first run—things unraveled from there. This is a division rivalry playoff series (first time these two have met in the postseason), and it's going the distance. Game 5 Saturday night, 8 PM ET in Cleveland. The Guardians' season was 3 outs away from ending. Now they've got one more chance to extend a World Series drought that dates back to 1948.

tweets.text: The New York Knicks are tabling all contract extension talks, per team spokesperson: "As an organization, our entire focus is on preparing for the upcoming season and delivering another year for our fans to be proud of. As a result, we will not be negotiating contract extensions until later in the season and will remain solely focused on preparing for the start of the season."

supporting_stories.research_notes: New York released a statement: 'As an organization, our entire focus is on preparing for the upcoming season and delivering another year for our fans to be proud of. As a result, we will not be negotiating contract extensions until later in the season and will remain solely focused on preparing for the start of the season.' Karl-Anthony Towns is willing to take less than a max deal, but there's still a sizable gap. Josh Hart and others are also in limbo. The Knicks are the defending NBA champions, and they're telling their stars 'we'll talk later.' This is either smart—lock in on the season, avoid distractions—or a gamble that could blow up if Towns or Hart feel disrespected. The Knicks are trying to run it back, but they're doing it without long-term security for their second-best player. The historical parallel: the Warriors waited to extend Draymond in 2019, and it created tension. The Knicks are betting chemistry and a title defense are enough to hold this together until December.

supporting_stories.headline: MLB Proposes 154 Games, Playoff Seeding Twist

tweets.text: Major League Baseball proposed cutting the regular-season schedule from 162 games to 154 games in a bargaining session with the MLBPA today. Also part of its proposal: higher seeds in playoffs get to choose their opponents, and division series expand to seven games.

The NBA should do this in the playoffs: “higher-seeded clubs…select their opponents.”

Allow seeds 1, 2, and 3 to draft from seeds 5-8 in the first round. Then you could allow the highest remaining seed to choose its second round opponent as well.

Important because it creates incentive to fight for higher seeding during the regular season. And it creates more drama during the playoffs with teams having to choose opponents. @mlb has the right idea here.

supporting_stories.research_notes: MLB proposed cutting the regular season from 162 to 154 games in a bargaining session with the MLBPA. Also proposed: higher seeds in playoffs get to choose their opponents, and the division series expands to seven games. This is radical stuff. Kevin O'Connor jumped in: 'The NBA should do this in the playoffs—allow seeds 1, 2, and 3 to draft from seeds 5-8 in the first round. Creates incentive to fight for higher seeding during the regular season, and more drama during the playoffs.' The seeding-choice idea is borrowed from other leagues (NHL did it briefly), and it does create incentive—nobody wants to be the team nobody picks. The 154-game season is a bigger ask: that's 8 fewer games, less revenue, less inventory for TV. CBS Sports called it 'great in theory, but has a built-in roadblock'—the union's not going to give up games (and paychecks) without a fight. The 7-game LDS is interesting: it gives the better team more runway, reduces variance. But the players' union will want something in return. This is a negotiating position, not a done deal. The cross-sport parallel: the NFL's 17th game took years to get done, and that was adding revenue. Cutting games? That's a tougher sell.

beats.angle: The 154-game proposal—8 fewer games, less revenue, union likely to push back hard
beats.landing: This is a big ask—players aren't going to give up games (and paychecks) without getting something major in return

beats.angle: Higher seeds choose opponents—creates drama, incentive to fight for seeding, borrowed from other leagues
beats.landing: This is the kind of wrinkle that makes the playoffs appointment viewing—nobody wants to be the team nobody picks
